error_description: cblE is defined by homocystinuria/megaloblastic anaemia WITHOUT methylmalonic acidemia; the only supporting annotation is an explicit exclusion (0%), so high MMA argues against cblE rather than being associated with it.

A low/undetectable anti-GM1b ganglioside IgG titer is the normal state, not an immune-physiology abnormality; it was bridged through a top-level catch-all HP term to a disease whose immune defect (T-cell lymphopenia) this autoantibody test cannot show.

Suppressed C-peptide occurs only in the rare IGF-2-mediated hypoglycemia (Doege-Potter) of solitary fibrous tumor (<5%), and it is shown on a sample drawn during hypoglycemia, not on a glucagon-stimulation test of beta-cell reserve.

Hyperglycemia is central to T1DM, but this is a timed specimen of a lactose tolerance test, where a glucose rise is the expected normal response and the test is read for a flat curve (lactase deficiency); a 'high' here is not the same as baseline hyperglycemia.

Congenital myasthenic syndromes are genetic and seronegative by definition; the AChR-antibody phenotype is annotated as excluded (0%), so a positive blocking antibody points away from CMS toward autoimmune myasthenia gravis.

An HIV-2 antibody test establishes (and types) HIV infection, which is only a prerequisite for AIDS; AIDS itself is defined by CD4 count or AIDS-defining illness, so the test is attached to the advanced-stage disease term rather than to HIV infection.

Hypoglycemia is an occasional feature of this disease and is shared by >200 diseases, so a low glucose has almost no discriminating value; in addition the test is a timed sample after an unspecified challenge, not a baseline/fasting glucose.

Elevated VLDL cholesterol is not a feature of Johanson-Blizzard syndrome that I can confirm (the recognised picture is exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, nasal alar hypoplasia, deafness, hypothyroidism); the annotation has unknown frequency and I cannot tell whether it is a single-case finding or a curation error.

The supporting path is an explicitly excluded (0%) hyperglycemia annotation, so the inference is invalid as derived, even though insulin resistance/glucose intolerance is in fact reported in mandibuloacral dysplasia type A; the 4-hour OGTT timepoint is also not one at which hyperglycemia is normally assessed.

Hyperuricemia is a necessary risk factor for gout but does not indicate it (most hyperuricemic people never develop gout; diagnosis needs crystals/clinical attack), and the ABOVE_TARGET band is a treatment-monitoring band that only applies to people already diagnosed. The right object is hyperuricemia, or a risk relation.

ANA positivity is annotated as excluded (0%) for this disease, so the association is the reverse of what the source says; anti-Smith is also a specific ENA rather than the ANA screen the phenotype names.
A low or undetectable allergen-specific IgE is the normal, non-sensitised result; it says nothing about the concentration of circulating immunoglobulin, and 'low' should carry no phenotype at all.

C-peptide is expected to rise after a glucose load, so a high value on a 3-hour post-glucose specimen is not equivalent to the baseline phenotype 'elevated circulating C-peptide' unless judged against a timepoint-specific reference, which the mapping does not capture.

Hypoglycemia is a core feature of HMG-CoA synthase deficiency but it is fasting-provoked hypoketotic hypoglycemia; a glucose drawn 1 hour after an intravenous glucose load is the wrong setting to demonstrate it and a low value there has a different meaning.

Beta-hydroxybutyrate is a ketone body (small organic acid), not a protein; high should map to ketosis/hyperketonemia and low to hypoketonemia, and lumping both directions into one 'abnormal' term discards the direction as well.

The analyte is right for naive CD4 T cells, but the specimen is 'Body fluid' (e.g. BAL, CSF, effusion) whereas the phenotype refers to the circulating/blood naive T-cell proportion; it also covers only the CD4 subset, and CD45RA alone is an imperfect naive marker.
Hypoglycemia is a very rare (<5%), non-characteristic finding in congenital syphilis and is shared by >200 diseases; the test is also a post-challenge timepoint rather than a baseline glucose.

A single-frequency, single-ear threshold is one cell of an audiogram; on its own it cannot characterise the hearing loss, let alone a specific genetic subtype, and the source row actually describes a multi-test battery (OAE, ABR, tympanometry) that this code does not represent.

A low/negative Black Locust-specific IgE is normal and does not show an abnormal circulating immunoglobulin concentration; Schimke dysplasia's immune defect is T-cell lymphopenia, and the bridging HP term is direction-less and far broader than what an allergen test measures.

A normal phospholipid-antibody immunoassay panel does not exclude antiphospholipid antibody positivity, because lupus anticoagulant (a clotting assay) and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I are not covered and positivity can be transient; 'argues against' would be appropriate. A panel also has no single N result.

Hypoglycemia is a genuine, frequent feature of MADD, but a low glucose at 5 hours of a lactose tolerance test reflects lactose malabsorption or simply the late fall of the curve, not the fasting/catabolic nonketotic hypoglycemia of the disease.

The concept (hypoketotic response to fasting) is right, but ketones in MCADD are inappropriately low for the degree of hypoglycemia rather than below a reference range, and can be measurably present; 'decreased' as an absolute result direction misstates this. The code is also a LOINC Part (analyte only), not an orderable test with specimen and property.

A low or negative pathogen-specific IgG titer (Colorado tick fever virus) simply means no prior exposure; it is not a measure of total serum IgG and cannot indicate hypogammaglobulinemia or this immunodeficiency.
The mix contains two nuts (cashew, hazelnut) but also kiwi, tomato and sesame; a positive mix result cannot be attributed to nut sensitisation specifically.
A normal cat-dander IgE excludes cat sensitisation only; the phenotype covers all animal danders (dog, horse, etc.), so a single-allergen negative cannot rule out the class-level term.

Hypertension occurs in a minority of Carney complex patients (secondary to Cushing syndrome from PPNAD) and is annotated to ~380 diseases, so raised blood pressure carries essentially no information about this disease; a BP panel also has no single 'high' result.

Low thyroxine-binding globulin has no relationship to myelodysplastic syndrome; the link exists only because both sides were attached to the catch-all, direction-less term 'abnormal circulating protein concentration', which in the disease record must refer to some other protein.

The test reports CD19 cells as a fraction of cells, whereas the phenotype is an increased absolute B-cell count; a high percentage can result from T-cell lymphopenia alone. I cannot independently confirm the disease-side annotation for this very recently described disorder.

A hepatitis E antibody test has nothing to do with yellow fever; the generic 'viremia' term drops the identity of the virus, and an IgG antibody shows past exposure rather than virus in blood in the first place.

Suppressed C-peptide occurs only in the rare IGF-2-mediated hypoglycemia (Doege-Potter) of solitary fibrous tumor (<5%), and is demonstrated during spontaneous hypoglycemia, not on a 1-hour sample after an unspecified stimulation challenge.

The band is bounded by critical (panic) limits, 37-910, not reference limits, so it mixes normal counts with clear thrombocytopenia (e.g. 60) and thrombocytosis (e.g. 700); the result is called uninformative only because the wrong cut-offs were used, when the same value is fully informative against a reference interval. Units are also missing.
error_theme: critical limits used as reference band
